before.label: Environmental history
before.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model. Bullard’s environmental-justice inquiry and Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life histories broaden comparison toward unequal burdens, displacement and authority over historical accounts. Dust Bowl debates distinguish agricultural capitalism, technology and soils, federal intervention, regional scale and household survival; primary criticism and later social history complicate a single causal summary.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

before.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

strands.focus: Bullard joins environmental distribution with race, class and organizing capacity. The Alsen case distinguishes partial gains from unresolved health concerns and internal disagreement.

strands.title: Country, displacement and historical voice
strands.focus: Read Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life-history project beside conservation and settler-landscape narratives. Publisher descriptions support this bounded comparison; their full books and place article remain unread.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Changes in the Land (1983); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Agricultural culture, technology and regional causes
strands.focus: Worster argues for interacting natural and cultural forces while emphasizing agricultural capitalism. McDean criticizes his generalization, contests Bonnifield’s federal-policy account and favors Hurt’s regional specificity. These are competing interpretations.
strands.works: Worster (1986); McDean (1986), discussing books of 1979 and 1981

strands.title: Ecological adaptation and the promise of development
strands.focus: Worster acknowledges Malin’s ecological history but disputes explanations through natural storms and a passing pioneering stage. He distinguishes rival cultural values and varied regional entrepreneurial intensity.

strands.title: Regional boundaries and histories of staying
strands.focus: Compare McDean’s insistence on a specific Dust Bowl region, Fite’s call for northern Plains coverage, and Riney-Kehrberg’s household survival study in southwestern Kansas. Causal explanation, geographical scale and lived experience pose different questions.

strands.title: Wilderness, livelihood and different political contexts
strands.focus: Guha targets American deep ecology’s universal claims and conservation’s unequal costs in India, while acknowledging Naess’s concern about inequality. Cronon studies American sublime/frontier ideals and everyday responsibility, explicitly citing Guha in note28. Shared concerns about exclusion do not erase their different contexts or Cronon’s support for protected wild lands.

strands.title: Can biocentrism incorporate social criticism?
strands.focus: Johns’s abstract disputes Guha’s equation of deep ecology with wilderness protection and defends biocentrism joined to critical social theory against overconsumption and militarism. This is a named response; the article’s detailed reasoning is not newly verified.

strands.title: Cultural criticism and habitat protection
strands.focus: Sessions objects that Cronon underweights biodiversity and connected wild habitat. His claim that cultural construction conflicts with independent nature is a critical interpretation: Cronon explicitly defends nonhuman autonomy and wild-land protection.

before.label: History of science
before.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
before.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

after.label: History of science
after.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
after.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Merton; Thomas Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962); Steven Shapin and Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985). Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

after.relationship: Merchant connects the history of science with women and environmental questions
after.evidence_note: Berkeley’s retrospective documents Merchant’s cross-field contribution. The added primary excerpt, reprinted in 1991, supports her account of mechanical order, control of nature and capitalist development. It does not verify every gender claim or adjudicate criticisms of the 1980 book. Selected 2006 retrospective passages now clarify Merchant’s material/ideational argument and her response to named 1990s critics. Pesic’s 1999 author abstract supplies a competing reading of Bacon’s metaphor. These sources document disagreement; they do not settle Bacon’s intentions or independently verify early experimental practices. Later reception is not backdated into the mapped period.

verification.note: Expanded from publisher description to authorized full-book scan at https://www.environmentandsociety.org/sites/default/files/key_docs/carruthers_kruger_np_0.pdf . Read title/imprint, contents, acknowledgments ix–x, complete prologue 1–6 and epilogue 119–122 in text layer. Chapter bodies, most notes, archival evidence and images unread; scan OCR has occasional errors. Distinguishes resource allocation, racial exclusion, state politics and changing conservation strategies. Epilogue’s expectations after 1994 are contemporary projections, not a check of subsequent events or present law. Broad claims about San societies and earlier historiography not adopted. Limited primary reading does not certify every historical case.

outcomes.finding: Merchant’s later retrospective clarifies her material/ideational argument and responds to named critics; Pesic’s 1999 author abstract supplies a competing reading of Bacon. Carruthers’s full available review of Grove and selected Kruger primary passages distinguish colonial knowledge exchange, state policies, racial exclusion and allocation of benefits. Different scales and questions are preserved.
outcomes.research_limit: Merchant 2006 selected 513–519 and 530–533, with intervening textual argument and table not fully read; original Bacon editions and experimental cases not checked. Retrospective bibliography does not extend mapped coverage. Pesic 1999 publisher abstract only; body behind access. Carruthers’s 1996 review full available PDF text read with interleaved columns; Grove book body unread. Kruger authorized scan: title/imprint, contents, acknowledgments, prologue1–6 and epilogue119–122 read; body, most notes and archive sources unread. No full image collation. Broad historical generalizations and post-1994 projections remain attributed, not certified.
